title: Thoreau's sauntering
hook: in his essay Walking (1862), Thoreau praises going out with no destination

segments.voice: Yesterday, walking meditation: a short path, slow steps, turn and come back. Your line was this step. Did you feel the floor? Day one hundred thirty-one.

When did you last go out with no errand? Not to the store, not to hit a step count, not walking the dog on its schedule. Just out the door, turning left because left looked nice. For most of us, the honest answer is: a long time ago. Maybe as a kid. Now meet a man in Concord, Massachusetts, in the eighteen fifties, who did it for hours every single day, and thought it was one of the most serious things a person could do. He wrote an essay about it, printed in the year he died. Today's practice is Thoreau's sauntering.
screen: `NO ERRAND, NO STEP COUNT.` → `CONCORD, THE 1850S.` → `THOREAU'S SAUNTERING.`

segments.voice: Henry David Thoreau is best known for Walden, his two years in a cabin by a pond. But his essay Walking, published in the Atlantic in 1862, just after his death, may be the most fun thing he wrote. It opens boldly: "I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness." Then he says he's met only one or two people in his life who understood the art of walking, people "who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering." And he plays with where the word saunter comes from. One story, he says, is that it comes from wanderers in the Middle Ages who asked for charity on their way, they claimed, to the Holy Land, la Sainte Terre. So a saunterer is a Holy-Lander, and every walk can be a small pilgrimage. Another story he offers: sans terre, without land or home, and so at home everywhere. Here's the honest part. Modern dictionaries say nobody really knows where saunter comes from, and Thoreau's stories are almost certainly more poetry than history. He probably knew it. But look at what he's doing with them. He's saying a walk without a destination isn't lazy. It's a kind of pilgrimage, where the holy land is wherever your feet happen to be. He claimed he needed four hours a day of it to stay well in body and spirit. You don't need four hours. You need one walk where nothing is the goal.
screen: `WALKING, 1862.` · `A GENIUS FOR SAUNTERING.` · `HOLY-LANDER, OR WITHOUT LAND.` · `NOBODY KNOWS THE ROOT.` · then, large: `SAUNTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a walk with no destination. Settle, and breathe. Picture your front door. Now picture stepping out and turning whichever way looks inviting. No errand, no route, no timer except maybe a rough sense of when to head home. Notice what that feels like in your body: freedom, or a little itch to be useful. Both are fine. Choose when today you'll go, even for ten minutes. The bell holds the time.
Thoreau's sauntering. Walking with no destination, which he treated as a small pilgrimage with the holy land wherever you are. Today's word.
Your line: saunter. Today, go out once with nowhere to be. Turn where it looks good. Come home when you feel like it. Day one hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Many people who love Thoreau take aimless walks in his spirit, without a route or a goal, and his essay Walking is still widely read by hikers and nature writers.
